questions.stem: The suffix '-able' (as in readable, achievable, comfortable) typically indicates:

options.option_text: Capable of being / fit for / suitable for the action

questions.explanation: -ABLE / -IBLE — adjective-forming suffix meaning 'capable of being [verb]ed'. Readable = capable of being read. Achievable = able to be achieved. Audible = capable of being heard. Visible = capable of being seen. Convertible = able to be converted. -able usually attaches to verbs of native English origin; -ible attaches to Latin-origin verbs (visible, edible, terrible). The two are interchangeable in some words; spelling must be memorised.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which suffix is added to verbs to form a noun for the PERFORMER of the action (e.g., teacher, runner, actor)?
questions.explanation: -ER / -OR — agent suffix from verb → noun (the doer). teach → teacher, run → runner, act → actor, edit → editor, paint → painter. Generally -er for English-origin and -or for Latin-origin (though not always). Compare other agent-formers: -ist (artist, scientist), -ant/-ent (assistant, student), -ian (musician), -ive (executive). Confusion trap: in 'runner', the consonant doubles before -er (one-syllable verbs ending in single consonant after single vowel double the consonant).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The suffix '-ity' typically converts an adjective into:

options.option_text: An abstract noun denoting the QUALITY or STATE

questions.explanation: -ITY — Latin-origin abstract-noun suffix. Pure → purity (state of being pure). Active → activity (state of being active). Equal → equality. Real → reality. Brief → brevity (irregular). Compare other quality-noun formers: -NESS (kindness, happiness, darkness — Germanic origin); -SHIP (friendship, leadership); -HOOD (childhood, neighbourhood); -DOM (freedom, kingdom).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which of these words is correctly formed with a suffix?
questions.explanation: -LY — adverb-forming suffix from adjective: beautiful → beautifully, quick → quickly, careful → carefully. Spelling rule: when the adjective ends in '-y' preceded by consonant, change y to i + add -ly: happy → happily, easy → easily. When ending in '-le', drop e + add y: gentle → gently, simple → simply. -LY also forms adjectives from nouns: friend → friendly, day → daily — easy trap.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The suffix '-ous' (as in famous, dangerous, courageous) creates:

options.option_text: Adjectives meaning 'full of / possessing the quality of'

questions.explanation: -OUS — Latin-origin adjective suffix from noun. Fame → famous (full of fame). Danger → dangerous. Courage → courageous. Joy → joyous. Note spelling shifts: glory → glorious; victory → victorious. Compare similar adjective-formers: -FUL (helpful, beautiful — full of); -LESS (helpless, hopeless — without); -LIKE (childlike, lifelike — resembling); -ISH (childish, foolish — having qualities of); -Y (rainy, windy, lucky — characterised by).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Match suffix to its meaning — which pair is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: -CRACY (Greek 'kratos') = power / rule, NOT wealth. Democracy (rule by the people), autocracy (rule by one), aristocracy (rule by elite), bureaucracy (rule by office), theocracy (rule by religion), plutocracy (rule by the wealthy — note 'pluto-' is wealth, not 'cracy'). Other meaningful suffixes: -PHOBIA (fear: claustrophobia, hydrophobia); -CIDE (killer / killing: pesticide, suicide, homicide); -OLOGY (study of: biology, geology, sociology); -PHILE (lover of: bibliophile); -GAMY (marriage: monogamy, polygamy).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The suffix '-tion' / '-sion' forms what part of speech?
questions.explanation: -TION / -SION — Latin abstract-noun suffix from verb. Educate → education. Decide → decision. Communicate → communication. Translate → translation. Convert → conversion. Permit → permission. Choose between -tion / -sion is mostly orthographic — verbs ending in -t / -te take -tion; verbs ending in -d / -de or -mit / -ss take -sion. Other verb→noun suffixes: -MENT (judgement, payment, agreement), -ANCE / -ENCE (assistance, performance, existence), -AL (refusal, arrival), -URE (failure, departure).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The suffix '-ward' or '-wards' (as in homeward, inward, northward) typically converts a base word into which part of speech?

options.option_text: a noun naming the destination or direction of travel
an adverb or adjective indicating direction of movement
a verb expressing motion toward a particular location
a preposition linking two locations or positions

questions.explanation: '-ward/-wards' attaches to nouns or adverbs to form directional adverbs (move homeward) or adjectives (the homeward journey). Option A is wrong because '-ward' never creates a noun. Option C is wrong because it does not create a verb — 'homeward' cannot function as a verb.

questions.stem: The suffix '-ment' (as in achievement, disappointment, improvement) primarily forms which type of word?

options.option_text: an adjective describing a quality related to the base verb
an adverb indicating the manner of carrying out an action
a noun representing the act, result, or state of the verb
a second verb meaning to reverse or undo the base action

questions.explanation: '-ment' is a nominalising suffix that turns verbs into nouns: achieve → achievement (result), disappoint → disappointment (state). Option A is wrong — '-ment' never creates adjectives. Option D is wrong — reversing meaning is the role of prefixes like 'un-' or 'de-', not '-ment'.

questions.stem: The suffix '-cide' (from Latin 'caedere', to kill) appears in many English words. Which option correctly PAIRS a word with its meaning?

options.option_text: infanticide — the killing of elderly or infirm individuals
germicide — an agent that destroys disease-causing microbes
herbicide — a substance that kills insects in agriculture
parricide — the act of deliberately killing one's own children

questions.explanation: A germicide kills germs (microorganisms), making B correct. Option A is wrong — 'infant' (Latin: infant, young child), so infanticide is killing of infants. Option C is wrong — herbicide kills herbs/plants ('herba'), not insects; insecticide kills insects. Option D is wrong — 'parri-' derives from Latin 'pater' (parent), so parricide is killing of a parent or close relative.

questions.stem: The suffix '-archy' (from Greek 'archein', to rule) is found in monarchy, oligarchy, and matriarchy. What semantic content does this suffix consistently contribute?

options.option_text: the formal study or documentation of a ruling system
a system of rule or governance by a specified group or person
a written code of laws governing a particular community
a person who advocates for or actively opposes a form of government

questions.explanation: '-archy' encodes rule or governance: mon-archy (rule by one), olig-archy (rule by few), matrI-archy (rule by mothers/women). Option A is wrong — '-logy' handles study. Option C is wrong — a written legal code is a constitution or charter, not '-archy'. Option D is wrong — '-ist' or '-ite' form agent nouns for advocates.

questions.stem: A student writes four suffix-to-function mappings. Which one is CORRECT?

options.option_text: 'graciously' — the suffix '-ous' converts the word into an adverb
'beautiful' — the suffix '-ful' converts the noun 'beauty' into an adjective
'darkness' — the suffix '-ness' converts the adjective 'dark' into a verb
'carefully' — the suffix '-ly' converts 'careful' into a second adjective

questions.explanation: '-ful' attaches to the noun 'beauty' to produce 'beautiful', an adjective — this is correct. Option A is wrong: in 'graciously', it is '-ly' (not '-ous') that creates the adverb; '-ous' creates the intermediate adjective 'gracious'. Option C is wrong: '-ness' converts adjectives into nouns, not verbs. Option D is wrong: '-ly' converts the adjective 'careful' into the adverb 'carefully', not another adjective.

questions.stem: The suffix '-escence' (as in adolescence, luminescence, and efflorescence) signals which semantic nuance that '-ness' and '-ity' do NOT share?

options.option_text: a permanent, fixed, and fully established state of the named quality
the process of gradually becoming or beginning to exhibit a state
a measurable degree or precise intensity of an underlying condition
the scientific discipline devoted to studying the named phenomenon

questions.explanation: '-escence' (from Latin '-escere', inceptive suffix) encodes an ongoing or incipient process: adolescence = the process of becoming an adult; luminescence = the process of emitting light. '-ness' and '-ity' simply name a static state or property. Option A is the opposite — permanence contradicts the inceptive/processual meaning. Option C describes degree, which '-itude' (magnitude) or modifiers handle. Option D is the role of '-ology'.

questions.stem: Medical English borrows from Greek to encode pathological concepts via suffixes. Which row maps '-emia', '-uria', and '-itis' ALL correctly?
questions.explanation: From Greek: 'haima' (blood) → '-emia' (anaemia, leukaemia, septicaemia); 'ouron' (urine) → '-uria' (haematuria, glycosuria); 'itis' (set on fire) → inflammation (arthritis, hepatitis, bronchitis). Option D is the most tempting distractor because it correctly places '-emia' but swaps '-uria' and '-itis' — candidates who recall one pair but not both will choose D.
